title: Debugging JavaScript with DevTools
summary: Use browser tools to find the cause of a problem instead of guessing.
nestedConcepts: Trace requests in the Network panel

subtopics.title: Pause at a breakpoint
subtopics.explanation: A breakpoint pauses JavaScript on a chosen line. You can then inspect what the program is doing before it continues. It is like pausing a film to study one frame. Set breakpoints near the unexpected behavior and step through the relevant statements. For example, pause at the handler and inspect the value before the UI changes. For example, pause before the failing line and inspect the input value that reached it.

subtopics.title: Follow the call stack
subtopics.explanation: The call stack lists the functions that led to the current line. It is like a trail of footsteps showing how the program arrived here. Read from the current function outward to find the caller that supplied the values or triggered the behavior. For example, follow a function call back to the event listener that started it. For example, use the call stack to find whether a click or network callback started the function.

subtopics.title: Watch
subtopics.explanation: Watch values as execution changes state. The Scope panel and watch expressions show variables available at the pause point. It is like checking the contents of a workbench while a task is paused. Compare expected and actual values instead of guessing at the cause. For example, compare a variable before and after a reducer or state update. For example, compare a value with the expected result while execution is paused.

subtopics.title: Network
subtopics.explanation: Network tools show requests, responses, timing, and failures. They help distinguish a slow server from a rendering problem. It is like a delivery tracker that shows where a package is delayed. Check status codes and payloads, while avoiding the exposure of private user data. For example, filter network requests to find whether the response is slow or unsuccessful. For example, filter network activity to one request before comparing its timing and response.

subtopics.title: Remove
subtopics.explanation: Remove temporary logs, breakpoints, and debug-only behavior before shipping. They can clutter output, leak details, or slow a workflow. It is like putting away repair tools before returning a vehicle to service. Keep intentional diagnostics clear and safe for production. For example, clear temporary breakpoints after confirming the fix so later debugging sessions are predictable. For example, remove sensitive information before sharing a screenshot of debugger state.

foundations.overview: Browser DevTools help you inspect a page while it runs. You can pause JavaScript, read variable values, inspect network requests, and check layout. Think of them like a mechanic’s tools for examining a running car. Change one thing at a time, use evidence from the browser, and remove temporary debugging code before shipping.
foundations.whyItMatters: Focused inspection gives evidence for a bug’s cause and helps verify the fix. DevTools can reveal runtime state that static reading alone cannot show.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A mechanic checks the warning light and tests likely causes one at a time.
commonUseCases: Pause when a button handler receives an unexpected value.
Inspect a failed API request’s status and response in the Network panel.
Use the call stack to find which event led to a state change.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More console logs always make a bug easier to find.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A breakpoint and a focused inspection often show changing values with less noise.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A failed request must be a JavaScript rendering bug.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Network status, timing, and payload help distinguish server, connection, and interface problems.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Debugging tools can safely display any user data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Screenshots and shared logs can expose personal or secret values; inspect only what is needed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A breakpoint changes how the program normally behaves.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Pausing changes timing, so verify timing-sensitive behavior again without the debugger.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The Network panel shows only failures.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Successful responses, payload size, caching, and timing can explain performance and data bugs too.

keyTakeaways: A breakpoint pauses JavaScript on a chosen line.
The call stack lists the functions that led to the current line.
Watch values as execution changes state.
Network tools show requests, responses, timing, and failures.
Remove temporary logs, breakpoints, and debug-only behavior before shipping.
